article_title: Fostering collaborative and embodied learning with extended reality: Special issue introduction
citation: Jacob Fortman, Rebecca Quintana. (2023). Fostering collaborative and embodied learning with extended reality: Special issue introduction. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09404-1
title: Embodied learning taxonomy distinguishing sensorimotor engagement, gesture congruency, and immersion across four degrees (as reported by Johnson-Glenberg and colleagues)
description: The introduction reports, citing Johnson-Glenberg et al. and its 2017 update, an embodied learning taxonomy that "distinguishes components of embodied learning into three constructs": amount of sensorimotor engagement, congruence of gestures to content, and amount of immersion. Each construct spans four degrees, "the first degree being the lowest level of embodiment and the fourth degree being the highest." These formalized taxonomies and rubrics serve as design tools for XR learning designers and educators.
requirements: Used by XR learning designers and educators to characterize embodied learning designs
A taxonomy such as QUIVRR builds on embodied cognition research to guide evaluation
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners in XR-supported embodied learning settings
target_learning_goals: Supporting embodiment-based science, engineering, and mathematics learning designs
key_sources: Jacob Fortman, Rebecca Quintana. (2023). Fostering collaborative and embodied learning with extended reality: Special issue introduction. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09404-1

article_title: Fostering collaborative and embodied learning with extended reality: Special issue introduction
citation: Jacob Fortman, Rebecca Quintana. (2023). Fostering collaborative and embodied learning with extended reality: Special issue introduction. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09404-1
title: Design XR environments around pedagogical and embodied-learning considerations rather than assuming the platform itself determines educational value
description: The introduction argues that the educational utility of XR hardware depends on the applications designed for it, invoking the reported maxim that "platform is not destiny." It further endorses calls for XR research "grounded in solid pedagogical reasoning," urging learning sciences scholarship that examines how XR designs support robust conceptions of learning rather than novelty-driven adoption.
requirements: XR applications must be designed to instantiate pedagogical and embodied-cognition principles rather than relying on hardware affordances
constraints: Corporate platforms largely developed by actors such as Meta and Apple shape learner experiences in ways authors flag for critical study
target_learners: Learners in formal and informal XR-supported learning settings
target_learning_goals: Designing XR experiences that foster collaborative and embodied learning
examples: University XR adoption efforts including XR-enhanced online courses, a student-led immersive design initiative, campus-wide VR pilots, and VR classes in a digital twin of a physical campus
key_sources: Jacob Fortman, Rebecca Quintana. (2023). Fostering collaborative and embodied learning with extended reality: Special issue introduction. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09404-1

article_title: Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale
citation: Gandolfi, E., Soyturk, I., Kosko, K. W., Ferdig, R. E., & Clements, R. (2026). Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10619-w
title: eXtended Reality Presence Scale (XRPS)
description: The XRPS is a 17-item Likert survey (1 = Never to 5 = Always) measuring presence in XR experiences, built on Lee's (2004) construct and scored via Rasch analysis into three subscales: emotional connectivity, co-presence, and awareness of self. Example items include "I felt like I was with actual students in the classroom." This study validated it for immersive videos of gaming environments such as Minecraft.edu.
requirements: Requires polytomous Rasch modeling with a minimum of 50 participants for precise item calibrations, per the article's cited guidance
constraints: Item 4 of the co-presence subscale misfit in this context and was excluded; the article notes twitches-based attention measures are context-dependent
target_learning_goals: measuring presence in immersive video-based teacher education
examples: Administered after each of two 360-degree videos (real classroom and Minecraft.edu) watched by 91 PSTs in sequence
key_sources: Gandolfi, E., Soyturk, I., Kosko, K. W., Ferdig, R. E., & Clements, R. (2026). Measuring presence in virtual world teacher education: validation of the eXtended Reality Presence Scale. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10619-w

article_title: Impact of extended reality on robot-assisted surgery training: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Bickford Michael, Alruwaili Fayez, Ragab Sara, Rothenberg Hanna, Abedin-Nasab Mohammad (2025). Impact of extended reality on robot-assisted surgery training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02559-z
title: Extended reality simulators for robotic surgery training
description: Extended reality (XR) simulators, encompassing virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and mixed reality (MR), are tools for training robotic surgery novices outside the operating room. The article describes them as "safe, ethical, and repeatable alternatives that produce objective measures of performance and allow real-time feedback to trainees." The most popular simulator identified is the da Vinci Surgical Simulator (dVSS), with the Mimic dV-Trainer also commonly used across included studies.
requirements: Participants must be robotic novices who have never used a robotic surgical device, or have limited experience with robot-assisted surgeries.
key_sources: Bickford Michael, Alruwaili Fayez, Ragab Sara, Rothenberg Hanna, Abedin-Nasab Mohammad (2025). Impact of extended reality on robot-assisted surgery training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02559-z

article_title: From Virtual Reality to Reality: Fine-Tuning the Taxonomy for Extended Reality Simulation in Dental Education.
citation: Serrano Carlos M., Atenas María J., Rodriguez Patricio J., Vervoorn Johanna M. (2025). From Virtual Reality to Reality: Fine‐Tuning the Taxonomy for Extended Reality Simulation in Dental Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13064
title: XR-simulation taxonomy for dental education along the virtuality continuum
description: The article proposes a uniform taxonomy for extended reality (XR) simulation in dental education, categorising 141 reviewed articles into Virtual Reality (VR), Mixed Reality (MR), Augmented Reality (AR), Augmented Virtuality (AV) and Computer Simulation (CS). The taxonomy is built on recurring features identified across the literature: 'stereoscopic (3D) vision, users' immersion, interaction, modification possibilities and the presence of haptic feedback'. These features serve as 'building blocks' for general definitions of each category within the virtuality continuum, adapted from Milgram & Kishino.
requirements: Each study must include a theoretical description of XR and/or the investigated ITT to be categorised within the taxonomy.
constraints: The taxonomy was developed for dental/maxillofacial education and does not summarise learning outcomes or the effect of technology components on the learning process.
target_learning_goals: preclinical and clinical skills training using digital simulation
key_sources: Serrano Carlos M., Atenas María J., Rodriguez Patricio J., Vervoorn Johanna M. (2025). From Virtual Reality to Reality: Fine‐Tuning the Taxonomy for Extended Reality Simulation in Dental Education. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13064

article_title: Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review.
citation: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w
title: Successful integration of XR into surgical training requires careful curriculum design and resource allocation
description: The review concludes that adopting XR in surgical training is not just a matter of acquiring technology: "The successful integration of XR into surgical training necessitates careful curriculum design and resource allocation." It further states that adoption is facilitated by designing user-friendly interfaces and positive social influences, while financial and resource challenges must be overcome. The principle directs programs to plan curricula and allocate resources when introducing XR.
constraints: The review notes financial and resource challenges must be overcome for XR to realize its potential in surgical training
examples: The review's conclusion recommends that future research focus on overcoming financial and resource barriers so XR can fully realize its potential in surgical training.
key_sources: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w

article_title: Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review.
citation: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w
title: Extended reality (VR, AR, MR) simulation systems for surgical training
description: Extended reality comprises virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality technologies applied to surgical training. The article defines them: "VR tools immerse users in fully digital environments", "AR overlays digital content onto the real-world environment", and MR "blends both VR and AR, where digital and physical elements coexist and interact in real time." The review catalogs named simulators (e.g., LapSim, LAP Mentor, Eyesi, Microsoft HoloLens, da Vinci VR) used across specialties.
requirements: Resource availability and addressing technical and financial limitations for effective use
constraints: Included reviews note limitations such as lack of realistic haptic feedback in some VR simulators and lower realism of AR training compared to box trainers
target_learning_goals: nontechnical skills such as teamwork and decision-making
examples: Included reviews describe VR arthroscopy simulators (ARTHRO VR, ArthroS VR), laparoscopic simulators (LapSim, MIST-VR), ophthalmic simulators (Eyesi), and AR head-mounted displays (Microsoft HoloLens, Google Glass).
key_sources: Esmaeel T, Elham T, Fereidooni Mahsa, Ayatollahi Haleh. (2024). Acceptance and use of extended reality in surgical training: an umbrella review. Systematic Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-024-02723-w

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: XReality framework classifying computer-enhanced realities by whether the real-world environment remains part of the experience
description: The XReality framework, attributed in the review to Rauschnabel et al., classifies computer-enhanced realities by whether the real-world environment remains part of the learning experience. If the real-world environment is at least visually part of the experience, the technology is augmented reality; otherwise it is virtual reality. The review quotes AR as "represents a combination of real and virtual content that is displayed in real time". Within the framework, assisted reality (text-based instructions overlaid on the physical environment) and mixed reality (seamless integration of more complex virtual and real objects) are subtypes of AR, and the term extended reality is suggested to be avoided.
requirements: The real-world environment must be at least visually part of the learning experience for a technology to count as augmented reality rather than virtual reality.
constraints: The framework suggests the umbrella term extended reality (XR) be completely avoided because VR does not extend the real-world environment but replaces its visual aspects.
target_learners: physics students at school and university level
target_learning_goals: distinguishing AR from VR and related reality technologies when selecting tools for physics instruction
examples: The review uses the framework operationally: reviewed papers were excluded when "the given educational technology does not constitute AR as defined in the XReality framework".
key_sources: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661

article_title: Extended reality and web-based imaging in case-based anatomy education: a two-year study of knowledge retention on anomalies and variations.
citation: Aytaç Güneş, Kalehuawehe Kalāwena, Pagat Shawnea, Oktay Cemil, Rettenmeier Christoph, Lee U-Young, Romine Rebecca, Lozanoff Scott. (2026). Extended reality and web-based imaging in case-based anatomy education: a two-year study of knowledge retention on anomalies and variations. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09470-7
title: XR-CBL anatomy modules combining donor-derived MRI, 3D photogrammetric and segmented models, and zSpace desktop XR in the gross anatomy laboratory
description: The article developed case-based learning modules for two abdominal conditions (Chilaiditi Syndrome and Mobile Caecum), delivered during a 2-hour gross anatomy laboratory via the Anatomy XRCore web platform on zSpace desktop XR workstations. The article states: "The XR hardware consisted of a stereoscopic display, infrared-tracked polarized 3D glasses, and an infrared-tracked stylus pen, enabling learners to actively manipulate three-dimensional anatomical models and donor-derived MRI datasets." Students in small groups (n = 5–6 per system) rotated, zoomed, labeled structures, and virtually cut through MRI planes while alternating with routine dissection.
requirements: Web-based DICOM viewer access to donor MRI scans, 3D reconstructions, case objectives, and clinical prompts
Faculty facilitators and teaching assistants to guide discussion and support technical interaction
constraints: Desktop-based XR rather than head-mounted displays, so no full immersion
Students had prior longitudinal exposure to the zSpace display and MRI viewer in earlier modules
target_learning_goals: Recognizing abdominal anatomical variations and anomalies
Interpreting MRI scans and 3D anatomical renderings
examples: Students generated initial hypotheses from history and physical examination findings via Google Forms, then interpreted images on XR-compatible computers within lab groups
key_sources: Aytaç Güneş, Kalehuawehe Kalāwena, Pagat Shawnea, Oktay Cemil, Rettenmeier Christoph, Lee U-Young, Romine Rebecca, Lozanoff Scott. (2026). Extended reality and web-based imaging in case-based anatomy education: a two-year study of knowledge retention on anomalies and variations.
